What happens to your money over a season?

We played a season of 250 bets 10,000 times on a computer, starting with $10,000, and counted how the money ended up. “Middle result” is the result in the middle; “usually between” covers the middle 8 times out of 10. “Ahead” means finishing with more than the $10,000 you started with. “Worst dip” is the typical biggest fall from your highest point along the way. The “sized to the edge” way of betting grows the bet when the edge is bigger and shrinks it when the edge is smaller (a standard sizing rule called half-Kelly); it never puts more than 10% of what you have on one bet. How it works →

An example to show what an edge does — and what no edge does. This is not our record. Our record is the picks above; it is too short so far to run this on.

With a real edge — same $100 every betWinning 55 times in 100 at −110 odds. Middle result: $11,155 (usually $9,245–$13,064). Ahead 81 times in 100. Typical worst dip 11%.
With a real edge — bet sized to the edgeSame 55-in-100 edge. Middle result: $12,609 (usually $7,453–$21,332). Ahead 73 times in 100. Typical worst dip 31% — higher in the middle, but wilder both ways.
No edge at all — same $100 every betA coin flip at −110 odds. Middle result: $8,864 (usually $6,955–$10,773). Ahead 23 times in 100. The book’s price quietly eats the money.
No edge at all — bet sized to the edgeWith no edge showing, this way of betting places no bets at all. You keep your $10,000. Not betting beats betting when the price is not in your favor.
Edge claimed, but not real — bet sized to the edgeBetting as if the 55-in-100 edge were real, when it is not. Middle result: $9,198 (usually $5,437–$15,561). Ahead 42 times in 100. Typical worst dip 39%. Sizing bets for an edge you do not have loses faster than flat betting — this is why we do not size bets on our chances until the record proves them.

Our picks, run this way: 0 graded picks so far (Nov 6, 2026). We need 30 graded picks before this runs on our own record. Check back as the record grows.

Even a small real edge comes with big swings. Nothing here is a promise that any way of betting wins.

How it works, in plain words.

This site helps you judge a bet before you place it. It gives a chance for every game and every player pick. It scores a whole ticket from any book. It runs a ticket 10,000 times to show how often it wins. And it keeps a public record of how its picks did.

The numbers are early. They’re still proving themselves. So Our record shows every settled pick with its result and date. Look there before you trust any number here.

Game forecasts (Who wins?)

Each game gets one headline number: the team we think wins, and how often we think it wins — for example, “Knicks 87%”. Under it, Model A (ALL_IN) and Model B (FULL_SLATE) show the two numbers behind it, where their numbers are in this snapshot. Model A is built by Grok and Model B is built by Muse. A game close to 50-50 is marked as a close call — a lean, not a pick to lean on.

A chance comes from past games. How well teams score and stop the other team. Recent form. Rest. Playing at home. Recent games count most. News that comes after the numbers are made — injuries, late lineup changes — isn't in them. So check the news before you use a pick. Every number carries its date.

Player picks

Player picks give a chance a player goes over or under a line. Points, shots on goal, catches and yards, and more. The chance comes from recent games — the most recent ones count most. It also looks at how good the other team's defense is against that kind of player. Warnings flag injuries and other reasons to be careful.

Touchdown picks work the same way. How often a player gets the ball near the goal line. Plus the weather and how the game should play out. The chance shown is our guess, not a book's price. Hold it next to a real payout and see if the payout is worth it.

Picks in the same game can affect each other. If teammates are on the same ticket, one scoring can make the other less likely. So the real chance of the whole ticket is lower than just combining the single chances. The ticket checker flags it when that happens.

The ticket checker (Check my ticket)

What “good value” means. Flip a coin with me. Heads, I pay you $2. Tails, you pay me $1. You'd take that all day, right? That's a good-value bet. The price is wrong in your favor. Now flip it. Heads you win $1, tails you lose $2. You'd walk away. Same coin, different price. A good-value bet pays you more than it should for how often it wins.

How it works. Upload a screenshot of a slip from any book. The checker lists the picks it found. You can fix any of them by hand: player, kind of pick, line, over or under. The chance for each pick comes from our board — you never type one in. A pick we have no chance for is left out of the score, and named. Enter the payout exactly as shown on your slip. Your screenshot stays on your phone. Nothing gets sent anywhere. FanDuel's board is the reference for what a fair price looks like. But you can bet wherever you want.

The score. The score runs 0 to 100. A 50 means a fair bet — the payout matches how often it wins. The score is 50 plus the value. A ticket worth 20% more than a fair price scores 70. One worth 15% less scores 35. It stops at 0 and 100. Next to the score you get the value as a percentage, and the chance the whole ticket hits as "1 in N". Like 1 in 7 — it should hit about once in every seven tries. There's no thumbs-up or thumbs-down. The score has no graded record yet, so it's just a number. One plain sentence sums up the verdict. Each pick shows our chance next to what the ticket pays like, so you can see which pick is carrying the ticket. If missing one pick still pays a little, the score counts that too. That's an average over many repeats of the same ticket. A single ticket either wins it all or loses it all.

The parlay simulator (Try a ticket 10,000 times)

The ticket checker scores a ticket you already have. The simulator is different. Pick legs from today's board — teams to win, plus player picks — and it runs that ticket 10,000 times before you place it once. You see the chance the whole ticket hits. How often you get 3 out of 4 right — the most common way to lose a 4-leg ticket. And what you'd win or lose on average per $100 at the payout your book shows. It also shows how wild the ride is. One ticket is all or nothing, so the average only shows up over many tries. Legs we can't match to today's board are left out and named. So the chance shown is only for the legs that ran. Never the whole ticket.

Game legs in the same game run on the same simulated game, so their link is built in. Player picks in the same game as another leg are different. That link isn't modelled here. The simulator says so plainly, and you should treat the chance as the best case. Spread and total legs aren't offered on the site. The full simulator, which includes them, runs behind the scenes. Every chance comes from our models, from the board's date. A leg with no model chance is never offered.

Your money over a season

Our record also shows what happens to $10,000 over a season of 250 bets, played 10,000 times on a computer. Two ways of betting: the same $100 on every bet, and a bet sized to the edge. Bigger when the edge is bigger, smaller when it’s smaller, never more than 10% of what you have. That’s a standard sizing rule called half-Kelly. These numbers are a teaching example, not our record. One row shows a real edge (winning 55 times in 100 at −110 odds). One row shows the same bets with no edge at all. One row shows what happens when you size bets for an edge you don’t have. Our own picks will run through the same simulation once 30 of them are graded. Until then that part of the page says so plainly. No way of betting shown here is a promise it wins. Even with a real edge, the sized bets end higher in the middle but finish ahead less often and dip further along the way.

Our Models

These are the 30 models behind the numbers on this site — 29 Mordy models (together, Model B — FULL_SLATE) plus ALL_IN (Model A) as the 30th. Each one focuses on one job:

Each number below comes from testing the model on past seasons it had never seen. For win/loss models, the score is log loss. That's how far the model's chances were from what actually happened. Lower is better. For totals and spreads, the score is the average miss in points. Lower is better. R² says how much of the result the model explains versus a simple average. Higher is better. Recalibration means we adjusted the model's chances using past seasons, so the quoted chance matches how often it actually hit.

  • Game (6 models) — walk-forward log loss: NFL 0.6429, CFB 0.5709, NBA 0.6260, MLB 0.6795, NHL 0.6690, CBB 0.5081. None has beaten the book’s odds across multiple seasons.
  • Touchdowns (1) — walk-forward log loss 0.4798, beats the position base rate in all 6 seasons. Probability skill only — no edge claimed.
  • Player props (9) — every probability passes walk-forward recalibration before it is quoted; e.g. receiving yards R² 0.331 vs trailing-average 0.240.
  • Totals (4) — walk-forward MAE: NFL 10.749, CFB 13.18, CBB 13.751, NBA 14.834 (v2, not yet wired into the board). Forecasters only.
  • Spreads (3) — walk-forward MAE: NFL 10.272, CFB 13.99, CBB 10.183. Forecasters only.
  • Soccer (6) — one per league; best is Eredivisie, which beat the market in 1 of 5 seasons. Forecasters only, no public track record.
  • Model A — ALL_IN (1, the 30th model) — a second forecasting source; the headline number is the average of the two models where both exist.

Every model gets tested on past games before it goes live. And we keep score in Our Record, so you can see how they've done.
